## About this series
This series is adapted from my 2017 lecture notes, *Introduction to Statistical Tests* ([original PDF](/assets/docs/statests.pdf)). [Part 6](../stats-6-proportions/index.qmd) introduced the $\chi^2$ statistic and the test for one proportion. This part uses the same machinery for three further questions.
:::

```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)

# A shared look for the figures in this series
accent <- "#8c2f39"; gold <- "#b08d4a"; ink <- "#5d6070"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFDF8", colour = NA),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#EEEAE0", linewidth = 0.3),
          plot.title.position = "plot")
)
```

## Do several samples share one proportion?

Imagine exit polls from four polling stations, reporting how many of the people questioned declared support for a candidate:

| | Station 1 | Station 2 | Station 3 | Station 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| declared support | 55 | 75 | 455 | 45 |
| people questioned | 100 | 150 | 1000 | 87 |

Is the structure of support the same everywhere, or do the stations differ? The null hypothesis is that all four share a single underlying proportion. `prop.test()`, which we used for one proportion, accepts vectors:

```{r four-sites}
support <- c(55, 75, 455, 45)
total   <- c(100, 150, 1000, 87)

prop.test(support, total)
```

The p-value is well above 0.05, so we have no reason to think the stations differ. The observed proportions all lie between 45% and 55%, and with samples this small, differences of that size are unremarkable.

## Is the die fair? Goodness of fit

A **goodness-of-fit test** asks whether the counts we observe across several categories fit a *specified* distribution. This is handy when visiting a casino, or when playing dice with a stranger. We throw a die 61 times and get:

```{r dice}
faces   <- 1:6
results <- c(7, 14, 9, 11, 15, 5)       # counts of one ... six
expected <- sum(results) / 6

data.frame(face = faces, observed = results, expected = round(expected, 1))
chisq.test(x = results, p = rep(1/6, 6))
```

$H_0$ says the die is fair: each face has probability 1/6. The test has $6 - 1 = 5$ degrees of freedom, and the p-value is large, so we have no evidence of cheating. Alea iacta est.

But beware of reading "no evidence" as "fair". Sixty-one throws is not many. If we saw the *same proportions* in ten times as many throws, would the verdict change?

```{r dice-more}
chisq.test(x = results * 10, p = rep(1/6, 6))$p.value
```

Now the p-value is tiny. Same die, same pattern, ten times more data: the test is much more powerful, and the pattern that was compatible with chance is no longer so. A non-significant result means we did not collect enough evidence, not that the null hypothesis is true.

```{r dice-plot}
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of observed counts for faces one to six, with a dashed line at the expected count of about 10 per face."
ggplot(data.frame(face = factor(faces), n = results), aes(face, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#d8cfba", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = expected, colour = accent, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Face", y = "Count", title = "Observed throws against the expected count for a fair die")
```

## Are two categorical variables independent?

The third use of the $\chi^2$ statistic is the **test of independence**. Say we want to know whether a new drug has any effect. We give the drug to 100 randomly chosen patients and a placebo to 100 others, and after some time classify each patient as *better*, *unchanged* or *worse*:

```{r drug}
trial <- matrix(c(21, 39, 40,      # drug
                   2, 45, 53),     # placebo
                nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                dimnames = list(group   = c("drug", "placebo"),
                                outcome = c("better", "unchanged", "worse")))
trial
```

The null hypothesis is that **outcome and group are independent**: treatment makes no difference, so the distribution of outcomes is the same in both groups. Under independence, the expected count in each cell is (row total × column total) / grand total, and the $\chi^2$ statistic compares that with what we see:

```{r drug-test}
test <- chisq.test(trial)
test
round(test$expected, 1)       # counts expected under independence
```

The p-value is very small, so we **reject** independence. The distribution of outcomes differs between the treated and placebo groups: the treatment had an effect. (My 2017 notes slipped here, phrasing the null as the opposite of what it is. The null is independence, and the test rejects it.)

To see *where* the difference comes from, look at the standardised residuals: the signed distance of each cell from what independence predicts, in standard-error units. Values beyond about ±2 stand out.

```{r residuals}
round(test$stdres, 1)
```

More patients than expected got better on the drug, and fewer got worse. Notice too that the four-station test earlier is the same test in disguise: a table with two rows (support / no support) and four columns, tested for independence of station and answer.

```{r same}
tab <- rbind(support, against = total - support)
chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)$statistic
prop.test(support, total, correct = FALSE)$statistic
```

## When counts are small

All of these tests use the $\chi^2$ distribution as an *approximation*, which is good when expected counts are large enough, roughly 5 or more per cell. With small tables, use **Fisher's exact test**, which computes the probability directly:

```{r fisher}
small <- matrix(c(8, 2, 3, 7), nrow = 2,
                dimnames = list(group = c("treated", "control"),
                                outcome = c("recovered", "not recovered")))
fisher.test(small)
```

Recovery was 80% in the treated group and 30% in the control group, but with only ten animals each the exact p-value is just above 0.05, and the confidence interval for the odds ratio is huge. A big apparent effect in a small sample is exactly what low power looks like.

## What's next

We now have a toolbox for measurements (Parts 3 to 5) and for counts (Parts 6 and 7). The tests for measurements assumed normality, so what do we do when a variable is stubbornly skewed? In the last part we look at **transformations that restore normality**, and wrap up the series with a map of which test to use when.
